cue: The view is wide and coarse, the colours lean toward ultraviolet, and fast flicker is easy to follow.

fov.note: Worked out from the field of each eye, 156 degrees back from straight ahead.

cpd.note: Honeybee grating limit; bumblebees give about 0.25.

M.note: Peaks come from honeybee receptors; the mapping from camera channels is the app's.

uvBlue.note: A phone camera records almost no ultraviolet, so some of the blue is read as ultraviolet.

rate.note: A person's 60 hertz divided by the honeybee's 200 hertz in bright light.

blindAt.note: The two eyes each reach 156 degrees back, so the gap sits straight behind.

blindSoft.note: How softly the edge of the blind wedge fades.

field.name: wedge
field.note: Draws the blind wedge behind the bee.

spectrum.name: matrix
spectrum.note: Applies the bee colour matrix to the picture.

rows: A bee resolves about a quarter of a cycle per degree, where a person resolves about 60. The picture is very soft, and a flower has to fill several degrees of the view before a bee can pick it out.
Each eye of a honeybee reaches 156 degrees back from straight ahead. Together they cover about 312 degrees and leave a blind wedge of about 48 degrees directly behind the bee.

The three colour receptors of a honeybee peak at about 344, 436 and 556 nanometres, in the ultraviolet, blue and green. Bees can see ultraviolet but no far red. The view shifts the colours to match, and the app chose how the camera's channels map onto them.
bee.jsonl:German Aerospace Center (DLR) and Bee Sensory and Behavioural Ecology Lab 2026

A honeybee follows flicker up to about 200 times a second in bright light, and free-flying bees give about 100. A person stops near 60. The view divides 60 by 200 and runs at 0.3 of a person's pace, so the picture steps and lags behind the world.
A phone camera records almost no ultraviolet, so the app reads some of the blue as ultraviolet. The app also chose how softly the blind wedge fades, and how the wedge and the colour change are drawn.
